paras: The lynching of Milan Howard took place at the bridge over Bonfouca, in St. Tammany Parish, Louisiana, in June 1882, when about sixty men took Howard, a Black man accused of rape, from a constable and hanged him from the bridge. The parish paper approved the killing, and the parish later paid for his burial as a man "hung by unknown parties." Outside Louisiana the hanging circulated mainly as a joke item claiming that Oscar Wilde had watched it from a train.

According to the St. Tammany Farmer of Covington, Howard was accused of breaking into a house near the Bonfouca saw mills on Sunday morning, June 11, while the husband was away, and raping the woman inside. The paper described her as the wife of "a well-known citizen of Bonfouca" and said she could still scarcely speak. It added, on hearsay, that Howard had committed a similar crime in Alabama and was "believed" to have assaulted the daughter of Ingram, a Black fugitive killed in the parish shortly before.

Howard was arrested and examined before Justice Gusman, who placed him with a constable to be taken to the parish jail at Covington. On a Wednesday, which the Farmer did not date, the constable set out with him, and at the bridge over Bonfouca, half a mile from the start, about sixty "citizens of the neighborhood" took the prisoner. They tied a rope around his neck and threw him over the bridge, and the fall broke his neck. He was seized and killed at the same spot, so he was not moved elsewhere.

The Farmer said the "prompt action" met "general approval", though it also reported a "threatened rising among the negroes" at the time. In October the parish Police Jury allowed Wm. Gaines $5 "to burying Miia Howard, hung by unknown parties near Bonfouca," an item reprinted with the proceedings in later issues. No report of an inquest, arrest or grand jury inquiry into the killing appears in the coverage.

The Farmer headlined its account "Hung for Rape by Judge Lynch," called Howard "a negro fiend" and "the wretch," and in a separate paragraph remarked that the parish was "not a healthy summer resort for desperadoes," naming Ingram and Howard. Other Louisiana papers followed in the same vein: the French-language Meridional of Abbeville wrote that "le juge lynch" had disposed of Howard, and the Lake Charles Echo called lynching "the cheapest way to rid the world of such fiends."

Outside the state the story ran as a humorous squib, first found in the New York Sun on June 22, saying that Oscar Wilde had seen a lynching at Bonfouca from a car window. The squib was reprinted in the Sedalia Weekly Bazoo, the Silver State of Nevada and the Staunton Vindicator in late June. It did not name the victim, and it treated the hanging as a backdrop for Wilde's reaction.

The Sun's squib said the man was a preacher taken out of jail by a mob who begged for mercy and was hanged from a railroad bridge, details the local Farmer did not report; the Farmer instead described his seizure from a constable on the road. The local account is the more detailed evidence, and the joke item is the weaker source. The date is also uncertain: the Farmer's "Wednesday" could be June 14 or June 21, and the Sun's printing on June 22 fits the earlier date more easily if it refers to this hanging.

bases: About sixty citizens took Milan Howard from a constable and hanged him from the Bonfouca bridge (A3), and the parish later paid to bury him as 'hung by unknown parties' (A9).
Howard was killed by about sixty citizens who took him from a constable without lawful authority (A3, A9), in punishment for an alleged rape of a white woman (A3, A7).

The local St. Tammany Farmer report (A3, A2) is matched by the parish Police Jury's burial bill for Howard 'hung by unknown parties near Bonfouca' (A9) and by a separate French-language Louisiana brief (A7); a New York squib (A1) differs in details.
